title: History of the Clever Youth and the Greedy Miller

full_text:
In the outskirts of Cairo lived an avaricious miller named Shakir, who took an unlawful half-measure of flour from every peasant's sack as his 'milling toll'. When the poor complained that their children were starving, Shakir laughed: 'My waterwheel turns for those who pay my price!'

A quick-witted youth named Hasan resolved to end the miller's extortion.
He dressed in the fine wool mantle of a traveling merchant, bought two sacks of fine river gravel from the Nile shore, covered the top layer with white wheat grains, and arrived at the mill on a spirited mule.

'Peace be upon thee, Master Miller,' said Hasan. 'I have brought two sacks of rare imperial grain imported from Antioch. It is dry and fragile. Let us weigh it carefully, and take thy lawful half as toll, but grind the remainder with utmost delicacy.'

The greedy miller, eager to claim half of this supposedly valuable Antiochian grain, eagerly hoisted the sacks onto his stone mill without opening them fully.
He threw the lever, the heavy grindstones whirled, and immediately a horrific grinding screech shattered the air! The hard river pebbles chipped the millstones into jagged fragments, smoking with friction and ruining the expensive granite gears!

Shakir screamed in horror: 'Woe is me! My millstones are broken! What devil's seed didst thou bring?'
Hasan replied with calm innocence:
'Master Shakir, my Antiochian grain is simply firm! But since thou tookest half the sacks before inspecting them, thou art an equal partner in the grinding! Now, pay me the value of my lost grain, or we go before the Kazi!'

Terrified of the Kazi discovering his unlawful toll-taking, the miller pleaded for mercy.
Hasan agreed to settle on one condition: that the miller sign a binding covenant before the village elders to reduce his milling toll to a single fair cup per bushel, and provide free flour to widows for three years.

Shakir signed the covenant. The waterwheel turned once more, but now it ground bread for the poor with honest measures, proving that wit in defense of justice can shatter the stones of greed.
moral: Greedy monopolists who exploit the needs of the poor find their own cunning turned against them by quick-witted justice.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "History of the First Larrikin"?
options: Presence of mind and quiet wisdom triumph over brute strength.
Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof

By running away from every problem
